title: Charlie Work

jokes.text: Charlie frantically calling Frank before the bar opens, rattling off 'Pick up, buddy. Pick up, pick up, pick up!' with barely-contained panic — instantly establishing Charlie as the only competent one
jokes.setup: We're introduced to what should be a normal bar opening
jokes.punchline: Charlie is in full crisis mode before anything has even happened on screen, foreshadowing that this is entirely normal for Paddy's
jokes.explanation: The opening beat works as character comedy — Charlie's frantic energy before we even see the bar sets up the entire episode's comedic premise. Stronger on rewatch once you know how meticulously Charlie holds everything together.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Frank, pick up! Pick up, buddy, pick up, pick up, pick up, pick up, pick up!

jokes.text: Cut to the bar interior: chickens are everywhere. 'Oh, shit.'
jokes.setup: Charlie just told Frank he has the place looking 'pretty good already' and needs no one making a mess
jokes.punchline: He walks in to find the bar completely overrun with live chickens — the exact opposite of 'pretty good'
jokes.explanation: One of the best visual reveals of the episode. The 30-second gap between Charlie's confident phone call and his understated 'Oh, shit' upon seeing chickens everywhere is perfect economy — the horror is entirely in the juxtaposition. The visual of a bar filled with live chickens is absurd and immediately funny. The deadpan 'Oh, shit' is exactly right.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Oh, shit.

jokes.text: Mac and Dennis are painting a sign reading 'Carmine's: A Place for Steaks' while chickens roam the bar
jokes.setup: Charlie asked Frank to make sure nobody is at the bar making a mess
jokes.punchline: Mac and Dennis are not only there, they are actively making things worse with a fake-restaurant rebrand — surrounded by chickens
jokes.explanation: The visual layering here is excellent — the mundane act of painting a sign combined with live chickens wandering around and the total wrongness of 'Carmine's: A Place for Steaks' as a fake restaurant name. It's absurdist but grounded in character logic.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: No time to explain it to you, you wouldn't get it anyway.

jokes.text: 'Who gives a shit? We always get a passing grade.' / 'Yeah, we get a passing grade because I bust my ass to make sure that happens.'
jokes.setup: Mac dismisses the health inspection as a non-issue
jokes.punchline: Charlie reveals that the passing grades everyone takes for granted are entirely due to his invisible, exhausting labor — the entire gang's obliviousness to Charlie's work is the joke
jokes.explanation: This is the thematic spine of the entire episode delivered as a single exchange. The character integration is excellent — Mac's dismissiveness and Charlie's wounded pride are both perfectly in character. Sets up the devastating payoff at the end.

dialogue.line: Carmine's: A Place for Steaks.

jokes.text: The 'joke stool' — a stool with a nail sticking out of it, which Dee defends as 'hilarious' because it pokes people in the butt and they scream
jokes.setup: Charlie tells Dee to get the 'joke stool' out of sight before the inspector comes
jokes.punchline: Dee argues it's 'hilarious' — the joke being that this is Dee's idea of sophisticated comedy: a nail impaling a customer's buttock
jokes.explanation: The joke stool is a perfect Always Sunny gag — it reveals the gang's moral/intellectual bankruptcy while also being genuinely funny. Dee's earnest defense ('they got a nail right in the butt') and Charlie's accurate rebuttal ('that's not a joke, it's a lawsuit') is sharp character comedy. It also pays off beautifully at the end. High character integration because only this gang would have a 'joke stool' as standard bar equipment.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Yeah, we get a passing grade because I bust my ass to make sure that happens, okay?

jokes.text: Frank lost his shoes in the bathroom — not because he didn't know where they were, but because they were 'gone.' He flushed them down the toilet.
jokes.setup: Frank says he 'lost' his shoes in the bathroom, which Charlie assumes means he can't find them
jokes.punchline: 'When I said I lost my shoes, I didn't mean I didn't know where they were. It's just that they were gone.' He flushed them.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. Frank's pseudo-logical distinction between 'not knowing where something is' and it simply being 'gone' is a perfect Frank line — deranged but delivered with complete sincerity. The escalation that he voluntarily flushed his own shoes then provides the even better follow-up explanation about anxiety and control. 'Flushing things gives me control. It's a thing.' The rhythm is excellent, and it's deeply character-specific — only Frank Reynolds would do this and explain it this way.

dialogue.line: Charlie, we found a loophole in the system. Yeah, it's a closing loophole; It involves airline miles and points.

jokes.text: 'It's an anxiety thing, Charlie. Everybody's moving so fast all of a sudden, it freaks me out. Flushing things gives me control. It's a thing.' / 'That's not a thing.' / 'It's a thing.' / 'That's not a thing. I've never heard of that thing.'
jokes.setup: Frank has just admitted to flushing his own shoes down the toilet
jokes.punchline: He explains it as a legitimate anxiety coping mechanism ('flushing things gives me control'), then he and Charlie argue in rapid-fire 'it's a thing / that's not a thing' repetition
jokes.explanation: The 'it's a thing / that's not a thing' exchange is rapid-fire and perfectly constructed. Frank's pseudo-therapeutic language ('it's an anxiety thing') applied to the act of flushing his own shoes is brilliantly deranged. The repetition builds to a small comedic peak. This is quotable, character-specific, and original — the kind of line that gets repeated by fans. The economy is excellent; nothing is wasted.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Frank, Jesus Christ, man, where are your shoes?

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: I lost 'em in the bathroom.

jokes.text: Mac arguing that the word 'we' is confusing because 'how can a whole group of people have the same idea at the same time? What, do they just say it all at once? It's ludicrous.' — while Charlie is in a crisis trying to unclog a shoe-filled toilet
jokes.setup: Mac wants credit for the airline miles scam idea and is angling for it at the worst possible moment
jokes.punchline: His argument for why 'we' is a confusing word is itself ludicrously stupid logic, delivered with total sincerity while the bar is falling apart around them
jokes.explanation: Mac's oblivious self-interest at the worst possible moment is a classic Always Sunny beat. The pseudo-philosophy about collective noun confusion is good Mac-character comedy. The timing (Charlie literally digging shoes out of a toilet) makes it funnier.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: It's not hilarious, it's just a stool with a nail sticking out of it.

jokes.text: 'We'll go through the normal arbitration process at the end of this.'
jokes.setup: Mac is demanding credit for the plan idea in the middle of a crisis
jokes.punchline: Charlie casually references a 'normal arbitration process' as though the gang has established formal dispute resolution procedures — which is simultaneously sad and hilarious
jokes.explanation: The idea that the gang has established a 'normal arbitration process' for settling credit disputes is a perfect worldbuilding joke. It implies a whole history of exactly this kind of petty squabbling that has become institutionalized. Very economical — four words do enormous comedic work.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: Yeah, and when it pokes their butts, they scream, 'cause they just got a nail right in the butt.

jokes.text: Mac reveals he's been 'screwed at the last three arbitration processes' and needs Charlie on his side
jokes.setup: Charlie mentions the arbitration process
jokes.punchline: Mac has apparently gone through this exact dispute at least three prior times and lost every one — the depth of his chronic failure at claiming credit is revealed
jokes.explanation: Quick escalation on the arbitration joke — 'three arbitration processes' implies a whole history of Mac's failed credit-grabs. Good follow-through on the worldbuilding.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: You flushed your shoes down the toilet? Why would you do that?

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: It's an anxiety thing, Charlie.

jokes.text: The glory hole in the wall — Charlie put a cover over it specifically to hide from the health inspector the fact that 'we have a place for a person to get their dick sucked by a stranger'
jokes.setup: Mac removed the glory hole cover because he thought Charlie put it there by accident
jokes.punchline: Charlie's matter-of-fact explanation: he doesn't want the health inspector to see they have an installed glory hole in the bar
jokes.explanation: The glory hole being a permanent feature of Paddy's Pub, requiring a cover plate specifically for health inspections, is excellent dark Always Sunny worldbuilding. Charlie's clinical description ('a place for a person to get their dick sucked by a stranger') delivered as a matter-of-fact health code concern is what makes it funny — zero moral judgment, pure logistics.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Flushing things gives me control. It's a thing.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: That's not a thing.

jokes.text: Mac pivots back to the credit argument IMMEDIATELY after the glory hole revelation, saying 'Back to the credit issue... you just don't know what it's like to be overlooked.'
jokes.setup: Charlie just explained the glory hole cover situation
jokes.punchline: Mac is so self-absorbed that the glory hole doesn't even register — he pivots instantly back to 'you don't know what it's like to be overlooked' while Charlie is literally being overlooked (his work is invisible to the gang)
jokes.explanation: The irony of Mac complaining about being overlooked TO Charlie — the person whose work is entirely invisible to the gang — is a subtle but well-constructed bit. The abrupt pivot from the glory hole back to petty self-interest is perfect Mac characterization. Gets richer on rewatch when you understand the episode's theme.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Oh, son of a bitch. Did you flush your shirt?

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Yep.

jokes.text: Charlie's reaction: 'Oh, my God, that's exactly what's happening to me right now.' — said to himself about being overlooked, as Mac rambles on about credit
jokes.setup: Mac says 'you don't know what it's like to be overlooked'
jokes.punchline: Charlie, whose entire life is overlooked labor, quietly recognizes the irony while Mac completely fails to see it
jokes.explanation: One of the more thematically resonant laughs in the episode. Charlie's aside is perfectly timed and deeply character-specific. It doubles as both a joke and the episode's emotional core.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: like, how can a whole group of people have the same idea at the same time? What, do they just say it all at once? It's ludicrous.

jokes.text: The lights go out when Mac turns on the vacuum sealer — 'that could be the vacuum sealer. That thing probably pulls a lot of power.'
jokes.setup: The gang is already managing chickens, a fake restaurant sign, and a health inspection; they've also apparently brought an industrial vacuum sealer into a bar
jokes.punchline: Of course the industrial machine blows the power — another layer of chaos added to Charlie's impossible day
jokes.explanation: Functional chaos escalation. The power outage serves the plot more than the comedy, but it does land as another absurd obstacle Charlie must navigate.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: What happened to the glory hole cover?

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: I took it off. I-I thought you... you put it on there by accident.

jokes.text: Mac's plan: casually bring up his credit contribution to the health inspector, 'and then he won't know what we're talking about.'
jokes.setup: Mac wants to establish credit for the plan in front of witnesses.
jokes.punchline: His strategy for establishing credit is to mention it to someone completely unrelated who has zero context for what he's talking about — a plan that achieves nothing while making him seem insane.
jokes.explanation: Mac's plan to gain recognition through a baffled stranger is funny in its pointlessness. Reasonably funny character beat, though not as sharp as his other credit-seeking moments.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Oh, shit! This thing's tits!

jokes.text: 'Are you sure? Maybe he's a racist too.' — Frank's response when Charlie tells him to take down the 'Talk American' sign
jokes.setup: Charlie tells Frank to take down the 'Talk American' sign before the health inspector arrives
jokes.punchline: Frank's response isn't embarrassment about having a xenophobic sign — it's strategic: maybe the inspector is racist too and would approve
jokes.explanation: One-line joke with tremendous character integration — only Frank Reynolds would respond to 'take down the racist sign' with 'maybe the inspector is racist too.' Zero self-awareness, complete sincerity. The economy is perfect: six words reveal volumes about Frank's moral universe. This is the kind of casual monstrousness that defines the show at its best.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Are you sure? Maybe he's a racist, too.

jokes.text: Frank: 'Take it down, please, okay? And shoes... shoes, please? Find some shoes.' Dennis: 'How's this for shoes?' — Frank appears wearing something absurd (later revealed to be black-painted feet).
jokes.setup: Charlie has told Frank to find shoes before the health inspector arrives.
jokes.punchline: Frank's solution to the shoe problem is to paint his feet black — interpreting 'get shoes' as 'make your feet look covered' rather than 'obtain footwear.'
jokes.explanation: The reveal of Frank's 'shoes' (black-painted bare feet) is a great visual gag. It's exactly the kind of absurdist lateral thinking that characterizes Frank — he solves the problem of appearing to have shoes by disguising his feet rather than obtaining footwear. The Charlie reaction ('Aw, no, Frank. Come on, man! You're gonna get black paint everywhere!') confirms the visual.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Dee, shut up, shut up, shut up! That's, uh, G-sharp. Okay, I got it, I got it.

jokes.text: Mac's reaction to the vacuum sealer: 'Oh, shit. This thing's tits!'
jokes.setup: Everyone is scrambling to fix a power surge crisis
jokes.punchline: Mac's response to the industrial machine is pure childlike excitement — 'this thing's tits!' — completely disconnected from the emergency
jokes.explanation: Quick character beat — Mac's enthusiasm for machinery in the middle of a crisis is good but minor. 'This thing's tits' is a funny expression but not a crafted joke.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: actually, what I do is I block the vents to the furnace and that fills the basement with dangerous gases. Drives the rodents away.

jokes.text: Charlie sends Dennis to the carbon monoxide-filled basement to change a battery in the carbon monoxide detector — a detector that is alarming because there IS dangerous carbon monoxide
jokes.setup: Charlie casually asks Dennis to change a CO detector battery as a mundane task
jokes.punchline: He explains he fills the basement with carbon monoxide gas to drive out rodents before inspections, so the detector is working correctly — they just need to silence it before the inspector arrives
jokes.explanation: This is one of the episode's darkest and funniest reveals. The setup-punchline structure is elegant: 'change the CO detector battery' sounds like responsible maintenance until Charlie explains that the detector is alarming because he deliberately fills the basement with carbon monoxide. His matter-of-fact 'No, no. It's incredibly unsafe' and 'we can't be down here too long' are delivered as though this is OSHA-approved pest control. Deeply character-specific: only Charlie Work would involve a DIY carbon monoxide fumigation scheme.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Mac was doing that thing where he tries to casually bring something up to me, like I don't notice. Come to me like a man!

jokes.text: Mac is trying to 'casually bring something up' to Dennis while Dennis scratches Mac in irritation — 'come to me like a man. Talk about being tough all the time. Can't even look me in the eyes.'
jokes.setup: Mac has been trying to get credit for the plan all episode; Charlie describes him as trying to 'casually bring something up'
jokes.punchline: Dennis's response to Mac's passive manipulation is to physically scratch him — and Mac is bleeding — the passive-aggressive dynamic escalating to literal violence
jokes.explanation: Dennis physically scratching Mac is a great escalation of the running gag — the passive-aggression becomes literal. Dennis's 'I was irritated with you' is perfectly cold. Good character work between these two.

dialogue.speaker: Delivery Guy
dialogue.line: You want to eat here?

dialogue.speaker: Delivery Guy
dialogue.line: Uh, yeah, you know, it's a long drive back to Ohio and I figured I was gonna be here a while, unloading all these steaks.

jokes.text: Dee changes her mind about the joke stool mid-chaos: 'I've changed my mind about the stool.'
jokes.setup: Earlier Dee reluctantly agreed to put the stool away; now things are even more chaotic
jokes.punchline: In the middle of maximum crisis, Dee is relitigating the stool decision — her comedic priorities are hopelessly misaligned with the actual emergency
jokes.explanation: Quick callback to the stool that also serves to remind us it will return at the end. Dee's timing is perfect — the stool becomes funnier each time it's referenced against the backdrop of genuine chaos.

dialogue.speaker: Delivery Guy
dialogue.line: Four hundred? You ordered 4,000.

jokes.text: The steak delivery truck arrives — it's enormous and the driver announces 4,000 steaks were ordered (Dee apparently hit an extra zero)
jokes.setup: The gang ordered 400 steaks for a scam; a massive truck pulls up
jokes.punchline: '400? You ordered 4,000.' Dee accidentally ordered ten times as many steaks by hitting an extra zero
jokes.explanation: The 4,000-steak reveal is a good escalation gag. The 'Dee's oversized fingers' callback later confirms it as character-specific comedy. The visual of a massive truck in front of a dive bar is funny on its own.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: You guys used Frank's credit card, you bought a bunch of airline miles. You used those airline miles to purchase 400 steaks...

jokes.text: The delivery driver wants to eat at 'Carmine's' before unloading — 'It's a long drive back to Ohio, and I figured I was gonna be here a while, unloading all these steaks.'
jokes.setup: The truck is a problem Charlie needs to hide; the driver should leave as soon as possible
jokes.punchline: Instead the driver wants to dine in, treating the fake restaurant sign as real — Charlie must now run a fake restaurant while conducting a health inspection
jokes.explanation: The driver wanting to eat at 'Carmine's' is an excellent complications-compounding beat. The sign biting them in the ass is satisfying story construction. Charlie's visible horror at this new problem is the joke.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: you know, we basically had already explained it to you, so...

jokes.text: Frank has flushed his shirt — Charlie sees it in the toilet. 'Did you flush your shirt?' / 'Yep.'
jokes.setup: Frank had already flushed his shoes; Charlie told him to find a shirt
jokes.punchline: Frank has now flushed his shirt down the toilet as well — the anxiety-flushing has escalated to clothing
jokes.explanation: This is one of the episode's funniest moments. The setup (Frank flushed his shoes as an anxiety response) pays off perfectly here — of course Frank then flushed his shirt when things got more stressful. 'Did you flush your shirt?' / 'Yep.' is four words of perfect comedy. The escalation of Frank's anxiety-flushing from shoes to shirt, with the flat 'Yep' confirmation, is brilliantly economical. This is what running gag escalation should look like.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Or that Dee's oversized fingers could've accidentally pressed 'zero' again when she ordered the steaks online.

jokes.text: The Gang argues about whose plan it was: Dee blames Frank, Frank blames Dennis, Dennis blames Mac. Mac: 'Then why'd you scratch me?' Dennis: 'Cause I was irritated with you.'
jokes.setup: Charlie points out they didn't plan for the hungry delivery driver or the 4,000-steak typo.
jokes.punchline: Everyone immediately deflects blame onto someone else in a perfect circular firing squad. Dennis's reason for scratching Mac ('I was irritated with you') is a non-answer that reveals the scratch was simply petulant aggression.
jokes.explanation: Classic Sunny blame-deflection sequence. The circular denial is a reliable gang dynamic. 'Cause I was irritated with you' as a reason for scratching is a funny Dennis-specific detail — the kind of casual cruelty that defines his character.

dialogue.speaker: Delivery Guy
dialogue.line: Uh, this is an alley. I think I'd rather just sit inside.

jokes.text: Charlie's full plan explanation speech — he correctly deduces the entire chicken/airline miles/steak scam in one breathless monologue, stunning the gang
jokes.setup: Mac says 'with all due respect, Charlie, you don't even know what the goddamn plan is'
jokes.punchline: Charlie proceeds to explain the entire plan in perfect detail, including every element, using precise business logic — the man everyone dismisses as incompetent fully understands the scam they refused to explain to him
jokes.explanation: One of the strongest jokes in the episode, thematically. Charlie, who everyone treats as a dumb janitor, turns out to have fully understood (and kept up with) a complex multi-variable scam the gang has been treating as incomprehensible to him. The gang's stunned reaction ('Very good, Charlie') followed immediately by their attempt to retroactively claim they already told him is perfect. This inverts the entire episode's power dynamic in one beat and is deeply character-specific — it only works because of how Charlie is treated by the gang.

dialogue.line: Alan was let go on account of his leniency.

jokes.text: The gang immediately walking back Charlie's correct analysis: 'We basically had already explained it to you, so...'
jokes.setup: Charlie just perfectly decoded their plan
jokes.punchline: They immediately move to diminish his accomplishment: 'We basically had already explained it to you'
jokes.explanation: Perfect capper to the Charlie plan speech. The gang is constitutionally incapable of acknowledging Charlie's competence — the speed with which they retreat to minimizing him is both funny and kind of devastating.

dialogue.speaker: Health Inspector
dialogue.line: I assume all the toilets are in working order.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Oh, absolutely. Yeah, I wouldn't bother checking if I were you.

jokes.text: Charlie's rousing pre-inspection speech: 'A day that I pride myself on. A day that I've never failed on. And I don't plan to begin failing now. Listen to me and listen close, like you've never done before.'
jokes.setup: Charlie is in the middle of a disaster and needs the gang to cooperate
jokes.punchline: His speech is a genuine action-hero motivational moment — but it's Charlie, delivering it about a dive bar health inspection, to people who actively do not listen to him
jokes.explanation: Charlie's speech works because it's played completely straight — he genuinely means every word, and Glenn Howerton's (Dennis's) silent reaction is surely perfect. The joke is the gap between the epic tone and the mundane stakes. 'Like you've never done before' is the perfect finishing line because it acknowledges the gang's failure to listen without Charlie even realizing he's making a joke.

dialogue.line: Do I smell cheese?

jokes.text: Charlie's rousing speech: 'Today is inspection day. A day that I pride myself on. A day that I've never failed on. And I don't plan to begin failing now. Listen to me and listen close, like you've never done before. We are going to pull this thing off, so help me God.'
jokes.setup: Charlie has diagnosed all the problems and laid out the stakes.
jokes.punchline: Charlie delivers a full Braveheart-style motivational speech — invoking his personal pride, God, and history — about passing a health inspection for a dive bar crawling with chickens. The grandiosity is entirely mismatched with the stakes.
jokes.explanation: Charlie's heroic speech is funny precisely because it's completely sincere. He's not being ironic — the health inspection genuinely matters to him this much. The juxtaposition of Churchillian rhetoric with 'we need to pass the bar health inspection' is a perfect character joke. 'Listen to me and listen close, like you've never done before' is a great line — the 'like you've never done before' acknowledges that they never actually listen to him.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: Oh, no, he wants a turkey burger.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: What? Why?

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: I don't know. I offered it to him.

jokes.text: 'Oh, son of a bitch.' — Charlie's reaction after his speech, presumably seeing another new disaster
jokes.setup: Charlie just finished his empowering speech about pulling it together
jokes.punchline: Immediately something else goes wrong — the speech barely lasted a second before reality intervened
jokes.explanation: Classic sitcom button — the speech gets undercut within seconds. The 7-second timestamp gap between the speech and 'Oh, son of a bitch' is excellent comedic timing. Pure economy.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: He looks like a turkey burger kind of guy?! Oh, my God, Dee

jokes.text: The 'patio area' reveal — Charlie has led the delivery driver to a chair in a literal alley. 'Uh, this is an alley.' / 'I think I'd rather just sit inside.'
jokes.setup: Charlie has been hyping up the 'patio area' as a top-shelf dining experience, talking up the driver as a VIP customer
jokes.punchline: It's a chair in an alleyway. The driver flatly identifies it: 'This is an alley.'
jokes.explanation: The alley 'patio' is a great visual/cringe gag. Charlie's earnest VIP upselling and the driver's flat 'this is an alley' creates maximum cringe contrast. The beat before the driver speaks — where the camera presumably lingers on the alley — is part of the joke.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Don't ask questions, just moan a bit, after a couple of moans say, 'I'm sorry.'

jokes.text: 'Spends all day in a truck and he wants to eat indoors! Hey, the man needs fresh air!' — Charlie deflecting the driver's entirely reasonable request
jokes.setup: The driver says he'd rather sit inside after seeing the alley
jokes.punchline: Charlie, panicking, pretends the driver's desire for indoor seating is eccentric rather than completely normal
jokes.explanation: Charlie's spin on a truck driver wanting to eat inside as though it's some bizarre preference is nicely absurd. The logic inversion — 'spends all day in a truck, wants to eat indoors' — is funny because it's technically true while being completely wrong as a conclusion.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Hey, buddy, how about a courtesy cough or something next time?

jokes.text: The new health inspector — a woman, not 'Alan' — arrives. Charlie asks 'what happened to Alan?' She says he was let go 'on account of his leniency.'
jokes.setup: Charlie has been banking on a friendly, lenient health inspector named Alan
jokes.punchline: Alan was fired specifically for being too lenient — Charlie's main advantage is gone, and the new inspector is strict
jokes.explanation: Good escalation — the rug pull that removes Charlie's safety net. 'On account of his leniency' implies the bar has been getting away with things for years, which is itself a funny reveal about how terrible Paddy's normally is.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: I'm painting a shirt!

jokes.text: 'Do I smell cheese?' — the inspector notices something strange about Charlie
jokes.setup: Charlie is showing the inspector around
jokes.punchline: The inspector smells cheese on Charlie — a reference to the show's running implication that Charlie consumes large amounts of cheese, possibly as a lifestyle
jokes.explanation: Four words of perfect character comedy for fans of the show. The inspector smelling cheese on Charlie is a beautiful piece of lore-consistent writing. It's also funny as a pure non-sequitur to a new viewer but rewarding to fans who know Charlie's dietary habits. Economy is essentially perfect.

dialogue.speaker: Delivery Guy
dialogue.line: The steak is burnt to shit. It's not even what I ordered.

jokes.text: Charlie pickpockets the health inspector's car keys and slides them to Dennis: 'What are these? They're car keys, okay? Just picked her pocket.'
jokes.setup: Frank needs to move the steak truck but the inspector's car is blocking it
jokes.punchline: Charlie casually pickpockets the health inspector conducting his inspection without breaking his conversational composure
jokes.explanation: The casual pickpocketing of the health inspector — without explanation or hesitation — is excellent Charlie Work. The cool competence of 'just picked her pocket' as a matter-of-fact logistical solution is very funny. It's both criminal and completely in character for how the show operates.

dialogue.speaker: Delivery Guy
dialogue.line: this is the worst restaurant I've ever been to.

jokes.text: Dee offered the delivery driver a turkey burger because 'he looked like a turkey burger kind of guy'
jokes.setup: Charlie told Dee to pretend she's a waitress and take his order; they have no actual menu
jokes.punchline: Dee profiled the man as a turkey burger person and offered him something they don't have, creating an extra problem; Charlie's incredulous 'why would you do that?' is the punchline
jokes.explanation: Dee's absurd food profiling and total failure to understand the job she was given is good Dee comedy. 'He looked like a turkey burger kind of guy' is a funny specific — Dee's condescending confidence about her wrong read on the situation.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Give this to Frank. Tell him G-sharp. Then you got to paint him head to toe in black.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: Why would I do any of that?

jokes.text: Charlie's solution to the food problem: cook the steak on the furnace in the carbon monoxide basement
jokes.setup: They have no kitchen; the driver wants food
jokes.punchline: Charlie's resourceful solution is to cook a steak on the furnace — the same furnace filling the basement with carbon monoxide
jokes.explanation: Using the CO-producing furnace as a cooking appliance is a great dark callback to the carbon monoxide bit earlier. The fact that this 'solution' could poison the food adds another layer of unacknowledged horror that the show treats as normal.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: I said bar, bar twice!

jokes.text: Charlie instructs Mac to put the chickens in the vent and then 'count to 30, and then start moaning into it' — 'After a couple of moans say, I'm sorry.'
jokes.setup: Charlie needs a distraction in the bathroom to redirect the inspector
jokes.punchline: His plan involves a grown man counting down and then moaning 'I'm sorry' into an air vent — presented as though this is a completely reasonable tactical decision
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best and most original bits. Charlie's 'moan into the vent / say I'm sorry' plan is brilliantly absurd but also somehow logical within the show's universe — if someone in the vent is moaning, the inspector will think there's a person, and 'I'm sorry' creates maximum awkward distance from the situation. The specific instruction to say 'I'm sorry' after the moans is the comedic peak — that detail makes no logical sense but feels right. Original, perfectly constructed, deeply character-specific.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: A bit excessive? Yes, I know, but I'm a little anal when it comes to securing the perishables.

jokes.text: Mac counting down from 30 out loud while everything else in the bar is in crisis — we hear '28, 27... 23, 22... 19, 18...' during other scenes
jokes.setup: Mac was given the countdown task while everything else spirals
jokes.punchline: The countdown continues across scene cuts — Mac is faithfully executing his one absurd task while chaos unfolds around him
jokes.explanation: The structural joke of Mac's countdown running underneath other scenes is excellent editing/writing comedy. It creates a ticking clock (literally) while also being inherently funny that Mac is diligently counting down to moaning duty. The commitment to continuing the countdown across scene breaks is a formal comedy choice that elevates this above a simple gag.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: All right, all right, all right.

jokes.text: Mac moaning in the vent — the inspector hears it and Charlie covers: 'Hey buddy, how about a courtesy cough or something next time? I'm sorry. Don't be sorry!'
jokes.setup: Mac is following Charlie's instructions and moaning into the air vent; the inspector hears it
jokes.punchline: Charlie's response is to treat it as normal bathroom behavior and lecture the vent-moaner about bathroom etiquette — 'some people, they got like no sort of social boundaries'
jokes.explanation: The payoff to the vent moan plan is one of the episode's best moments. Charlie's improvised lecture about bathroom etiquette — delivered to an air vent while an inspector watches — is brilliantly executed cringe comedy. The echo of 'I'm sorry' from Mac fulfilling his exact instructions while Charlie scolds him for it has beautiful structural irony. The inspector's visible confusion and Charlie's smooth redirect to 'did you meet our bartender?' is a great comedic button.

dialogue.speaker: Sandy
dialogue.line: The regulation is exactly six feet and you were at five and a half.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Oh, that goddamn bitch!

jokes.text: Charlie to the inspector about the women's bathroom: 'We actually hardly ever have women in here, so...' presented as a point of pride
jokes.setup: Charlie is showing the inspector around
jokes.punchline: He casually mentions they 'hardly ever' have women in the bar as though this is a recommendation rather than a condemnation
jokes.explanation: Quick character-revealing line that lands as a minor laugh. The implication that women avoid Paddy's entirely is good dark observational comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Sandy
dialogue.line: Congratulations.

dialogue.speaker: Sandy
dialogue.line: Oh, my... You got me with the whole Dumpster thing!

jokes.text: 'Go ahead and tinkle. Move your bowels if you have to.' — Charlie inviting the inspector to use the restroom she's supposed to be inspecting
jokes.setup: The inspector is about to check the women's bathroom
jokes.punchline: Charlie, trying to seem casual, overexplains and crosses into absurdly inappropriate territory: 'move your bowels if you have to'
jokes.explanation: Charlie's social awkwardness under pressure creating an absurdly clinical overshare — 'move your bowels if you have to' is genuinely funny in context. It's the kind of thing someone says when trying too hard to seem casual, which makes it cringe in the best way.

dialogue.speaker: Health Inspector
dialogue.line: However, you do have an amazingly clean bar and therefore I'm giving Paddy's Pub the highest possible grade.

jokes.text: The furnace cooked the steak too fast — it's 'charred to shit'; Charlie instructs Dee to give it to him anyway and just tell him 'you got the order wrong'
jokes.setup: Dee needs to serve the driver food to keep him in the alley and away from the inspection
jokes.punchline: The 'kitchen' (furnace) has destroyed the steak; Charlie's solution is to serve charcoal and claim a wrong order
jokes.explanation: Functional escalation gag — the charred steak is a satisfying consequence of using a CO furnace as a cooking appliance. Charlie's nonchalance about serving inedible food is in character but the joke itself is relatively minor.

dialogue.line: Oh, yeah, we don't, we don't give a shit about that.

jokes.text: Frank emerges from the keg room painting a shirt onto his bare chest
jokes.setup: Charlie told Frank to 'find a shirt' multiple times; Frank's flushing anxiety has left him without clothes
jokes.punchline: Frank's solution is to paint a shirt directly onto his bare torso — this is not a shirt
jokes.explanation: Frank painting a shirt onto his body is one of the episode's most original and visually funny moments. It perfectly escalates the clothing-flushing arc to its logical extreme: Frank cannot have a shirt because he flushed it, so he paints one on. The image of DeVito shirtless painting a shirt onto his bare chest is pure physical comedy gold. It also demonstrates Frank's deranged practical creativity — it IS a kind of shirt. High marks across the board.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: We always pass, okay? We never have a hard time passing. It's not a big deal. Nobody gives a shit. You didn't do anything that special.

jokes.text: Charlie's fabricated 'outdoor liquor license' rule to force the driver inside: 'We don't have our outdoor liquor license. I gotta have you drink it inside.'
jokes.setup: The driver wants to drink his free beer outside (in the alley)
jokes.punchline: Charlie invents a fake regulation — an 'outdoor liquor license' — to get the driver inside; it works
jokes.explanation: Charlie's instant invention of a plausible-sounding fake regulation shows his crisis improvisation skills. The 'outdoor liquor license' is specific enough to sound real and is delivered with complete confidence. Good but not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: That's how you make a joke stool right there! That's... Ow, Charlie!

jokes.text: Charlie asks Dee about the Dumpster and she confirms she moved it; then he tells her to paint Frank 'head to toe in black' — Dee: 'Why would I do any of that?' / Charlie: 'Dee, just do it, okay? Just do it, you goddamn bitch.'
jokes.setup: Charlie is orchestrating multiple operations simultaneously; the black paint is for Frank to become invisible against the alley for the truck maneuver
jokes.punchline: The instruction to paint Frank entirely black is so strange that even Dee — who goes along with everything — objects; Charlie's breakdown into 'you goddamn bitch' is the pressure valve releasing
jokes.explanation: The 'paint Frank black' instruction is wonderfully absurd and implies Charlie's plan involves Frank using darkness as camouflage. His exasperated 'goddamn bitch' at Dee's entirely reasonable question is a great pressure-release moment for the episode's accelerating tension.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: That's how you make a joke stool right there! That's... Ow, Charlie! Did you do that?

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Yeah, you know what? I think I did.

jokes.text: Dee muttering 'Oh, that goddamn bitch. Oh, that goddamn bitch!' to herself as she runs down the alley after being called a bitch
jokes.setup: Charlie just called Dee a 'goddamn bitch' for questioning his plan
jokes.punchline: Dee immediately parrots the exact insult back at Charlie while running away — she's so rattled she's just echoing
jokes.explanation: Dee's self-deflecting mutual insult is a quick character beat. The parroting of 'that goddamn bitch' back at Charlie while running away is funny but minor.

jokes.text: Charlie steering the driver to the 'VIP lounge area' — which is clearly a corner of the bar with nothing special — using intense, possibly physical pressure to keep him away from the main bar
jokes.setup: The inspector is in the bar; the driver must be kept separate and occupied
jokes.punchline: Charlie's VIP lounge is a fiction delivered with maximum conviction — the driver's objection 'it's not a lounge' is overridden by Charlie's sheer physical and verbal force
jokes.explanation: The VIP lounge bit is a lesser version of the alley patio bit — same joke, slightly lower stakes. Still effective as a Charlie-herding-everyone bit.

jokes.text: Charlie shows the inspector the blender and voluntarily cranks it to its highest setting, blowing the power — again
jokes.setup: The inspection is going well; Charlie is wrapping up and showing off the bar's features
jokes.punchline: Charlie turns the blender to maximum despite knowing it blows the power — he does it anyway, apparently compulsively; 'that's why we never really do it'
jokes.explanation: Charlie voluntarily doing the thing that blows power — which he already knows blows power — in front of the inspector is a great controlled-chaos gag. His explanation after ('that's why we never really do it') is the perfect deflection. The inspector's dry 'I should dock you for that one. I'm not gonna. That's a joke.' is an excellent unexpected beat.

jokes.text: Sandy: 'There's drainage pipes down there that I don't want you to check.' Charlie panics. Sandy goes to look: 'Actually, they look pretty good.'
jokes.setup: Charlie tries to steer Sandy away from the drainage pipes by naming them specifically — the worst possible reverse-psychology move.
jokes.punchline: Sandy investigates and finds them fine. Charlie's panic was unnecessary AND his attempt to hide the pipes by naming them backfired perfectly — except it didn't, because the pipes are actually okay.
jokes.explanation: Funny structure — Charlie's specific 'don't check the drainage pipes' inadvertently draws attention to them, but the twist is they're actually fine. It's a double reversal (he panicked unnecessarily, the warning backfired but worked anyway) that lands as a moment of unexpected relief humor.

jokes.text: Sandy the inspector: 'I should dock you for that one. I'm not gonna. That's a joke.' — delivered completely deadpan
jokes.setup: Charlie just blew the power by turning the blender to max
jokes.punchline: The inspector makes a dry joke and immediately announces it as a joke — 'that's a joke' — implying she's aware of her own reputation for humorlessness or is uncomfortable with humor
jokes.explanation: 'That's a joke' is a quietly perfect line — the inspector labeling her own joke is both a character reveal (she's self-conscious about humor) and unexpectedly meta. It's the kind of line that gets funnier after the episode ends.

jokes.text: Charlie shows the inspector the keg room 'packaging operation' — which is now apparently a fully operational vacuum-sealing facility crammed into the keg room of a bar
jokes.setup: Charlie has been directing people to the keg room all episode with steaks, chickens, and packaging equipment
jokes.punchline: The resulting visual — an absurdly over-equipped industrial packaging station in a dive bar keg room — is what Charlie presents as his obsessive food safety operation: 'I'm a little anal when it comes to securing the perishables'
jokes.explanation: The keg room reveal is a great visual payoff to the entire episode's frantic staging — all the chaos Charlie has been orchestrating resolves into something that looks like a legitimate (if excessive) food safety operation. 'I'm a little anal when it comes to securing the perishables' is a great line for a man who has been using carbon monoxide fumigation. The inspector's impressed 'Oh my!' is the perfect straight-man reaction.

jokes.text: Sandy is getting light-headed from the carbon monoxide. Charlie: 'Yeah, it could be the stairs. Or, you know, maybe you're just dizzy by the cleanliness. Let's get you out of here. No sense in lingering around.'
jokes.setup: Sandy is showing symptoms of carbon monoxide poisoning.
jokes.punchline: Charlie attributes her poisoning symptoms to either 'the stairs' or being 'dizzy by the cleanliness' — the second explanation being a truly insane reframe — while hustling her out before she dies.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. 'Maybe you're just dizzy by the cleanliness' is a brilliantly specific piece of absurdist deflection — it inverts the problem (CO poisoning) into a compliment (the bar is so clean it's making you faint). The escalating specificity of Charlie's cover stories, culminating in this, is exceptional comedic craft. The dark undertone — he's casually poisoning a government official — fits perfectly with Sunny's sensibility.

jokes.text: Truck driver confrontation in the bar: 'We're not paying for contaminated steaks. Your entire truck is filled with chickens.'
jokes.setup: The delivery driver has presumably discovered the Gang put chickens on his truck.
jokes.punchline: The simple declarative 'Your entire truck is filled with chickens' — delivered as a complaint — is funny in its matter-of-fact acknowledgment of the insane plan's execution. The plan worked, but in the most chaotic way possible.
jokes.explanation: Good punctuation joke. The deadpan 'Your entire truck is filled with chickens' is funny precisely because it's a formal complaint about something completely insane — as if one might normally file this complaint. The situation lived up to its absurd premise.

jokes.text: The steak delivery driver confronts the gang in the bar: 'We're not paying for contaminated steaks. Your entire truck is filled with chickens.'
jokes.setup: The gang has been frantically moving chickens to the truck as part of the contamination scam
jokes.punchline: The end result is apparently an entire 18-wheeler full of chickens — the driver presents this calmly as though it's a complaint he expected to have to make
jokes.explanation: The reveal that the whole truck is now full of chickens is a good payoff to the chicken-moving subplot. 'Your entire truck is filled with chickens' delivered flatly is funny.

jokes.text: Dennis's response to the driver complaining about the insane restaurant: 'We get the drunks in here, they get all ornery and confused. What are you gonna do? It comes with the territory.'
jokes.setup: The driver says 'this restaurant is insane'
jokes.punchline: Dennis dismisses 4,000 contaminated steaks and chickens in a truck as the kind of thing that happens with 'ornery and confused drunks' — an utterly absurd non-explanation delivered with total smoothness
jokes.explanation: Dennis's smooth dismissal of an utterly insane situation as routine bar management is excellent deadpan character comedy. 'It comes with the territory' applied to a truck full of chickens is a great line. Dennis's sociopathic composure is perfectly deployed here.

jokes.text: 'You know, all right, all right, all right... kind of says it all.' — Charlie's reaction to Dennis's bartender performance
jokes.setup: Dennis has just given the most minimal possible response to the inspector
jokes.punchline: Charlie reads Dennis's cold three-word answer as a complete personality portrait — 'kind of says it all' — which it absolutely does
jokes.explanation: Charlie's aside about Dennis's 'all right, all right, all right' is surprisingly rich — it's a character observation that doubles as an affectionate audience wink. The economy is excellent and it rewards viewers who know Dennis well.

jokes.text: Sandy's final verdict: the Dumpster is six inches too close — 'The regulation is exactly six feet, and you were at five and a half.'
jokes.setup: Charlie has successfully navigated every obstacle — the chickens, the CO, the fake restaurant, the shirt painting, the vent moaning — and believes he's passed
jokes.punchline: He loses a point because Dee didn't move the Dumpster far enough — the one task he explicitly instructed Dee to do, which she failed at by six inches
jokes.explanation: Perfect structural payoff — Dee's argument about six inches of Dumpster placement comes back to bite Charlie exactly as feared. The specificity of '5.5 feet vs. 6 feet' makes it funnier. 'Oh, that goddamn bitch' — Charlie's internal monologue at Dee — is the perfect reaction line and callback.

jokes.text: Sandy: 'What's not fine, Mr. Kelly, is the Dumpster. The regulation is exactly six feet, and you were at five and a half.' Charlie: 'Oh, that goddamn bitch.' Sandy: 'I know Alan would let this slide, but I'm not Alan.'
jokes.setup: Charlie has navigated every obstacle: chickens, carbon monoxide, glory holes, steak truck, blender power failure.
jokes.punchline: The only thing that gets him docked is Dee's half-inch Dumpster shortfall. The callback to Dee's 'you think she's gonna notice six inches?' is the perfect dark punchline. Sandy's reminder that she's 'not Alan' closes the inspector subplot.
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's structural crown jewel. Everything works because of the callback: Dee said 'you think she's gonna notice six inches?' and the answer is yes, the new inspector absolutely does notice. The fact that Charlie survives carbon monoxide, glory holes, live chickens, 4,000 steaks, and a fake restaurant — but gets dinged by half an inch of Dumpster — is a perfect dark irony. 'I know Alan would let this slide, but I'm not Alan' closes both the inspector arc and the Alan joke. Near-perfect structure score.

jokes.text: 'Oh, that goddamn bitch.' — Charlie's inner monologue/mutter when the Dumpster is flagged
jokes.setup: Sandy announces the Dumpster violation
jokes.punchline: Charlie's response — an almost reverent 'oh, that goddamn bitch' — perfectly echoes Dee's own self-directed muttering from earlier, completing the callback
jokes.explanation: Four words serving as the perfect callback, character moment, and plot punctuation simultaneously. 'Oh, that goddamn bitch' has tremendous economy — it's the entire history of Charlie's frustrated relationship with Dee's incompetence in one mutter. High quotability; this is an instantly memorable line.

jokes.text: Despite the Dumpster violation, the inspector gives Paddy's the HIGHEST possible grade because of its exceptional cleanliness
jokes.setup: Sandy has just docked Charlie for the Dumpster; Charlie is bracing for failure
jokes.punchline: She gives them the highest possible grade anyway — 'you have an amazingly clean bar' — all of Charlie's insane work was genuine and actually worked
jokes.explanation: The highest grade reveal is an earned, satisfying payoff to the entire episode. It validates Charlie's competence and his exhausting labor — but sets up the final cruel twist. Structurally excellent: we're set up to feel Charlie's victory before the final devastation.

jokes.text: Charlie runs in to tell the gang they got the highest grade — the gang's response: 'Boo.'
jokes.setup: Charlie bursts in elated about the highest health inspection grade ever
jokes.punchline: The gang boos. They don't care about the health inspection at all — they're upset the airline miles scam didn't go through
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the episode and possibly in Always Sunny. Charlie has just pulled off an impossible one-man operation — managing chickens, carbon monoxide fumigation, a fake restaurant, a pickpocket, an industrial keg room packaging operation, a painted Frank, and a vent-moaning diversion — and his reward is a single syllable: 'Boo.' The gang's total indifference to Charlie's greatest professional achievement is both a devastating character comment and a perfect dark laugh. The structure of the entire episode converges on this single word. Exceptional.

jokes.text: 'We always pass, okay? We never have a hard time passing. It's not a big deal. Nobody gives a shit. You didn't do anything that special.' — the gang dismissing Charlie's achievement
jokes.setup: Charlie tries to explain what he just accomplished; the gang dismisses him
jokes.punchline: The audience has just watched 20 minutes of Charlie's superhuman effort; the gang has no idea any of it happened and believes it was effortless
jokes.explanation: This is the thematic punchline of the entire episode, delivered with perfect economy. 'You didn't do anything that special' — spoken by people who have no idea what Charlie just did — is the cruelest possible ending for Charlie and the most satisfying structural payoff for the audience. The episode is literally called 'Charlie Work' and this is the final statement on what Charlie's work means to the people he does it for: nothing. Exceptional character writing.

jokes.text: The joke stool payoff — Charlie, in silent revenge, places the nail stool under Dee as she sits. She screams. 'Did you do that?' / 'Yeah, you know what? I think I did.' Everyone laughs including Charlie.
jokes.setup: The joke stool was introduced early as a 'hilarious' nail-butt device that Charlie refused to allow
jokes.punchline: In the episode's final moment, Charlie uses the stool on Dee — apparently satisfying his own need for a small victory after being dismissed; the gang laughs, and even Charlie laughs
jokes.explanation: One of the best episode-closing jokes in Always Sunny history. The joke stool has been planted, teased, and held in reserve for the entire episode. Charlie, crushed by the gang's dismissal of his work, finds his small revenge not through words but through the one joke he refused to allow — now deployed on Dee. The fact that it makes EVERYONE laugh, including Charlie, is a rare moment of genuine gang solidarity. The structure is nearly perfect: an A-story setup (health inspection) and a B-story prop (joke stool) collide in a single image. The punchline isn't even verbal — it's a nail in Dee's butt. And it earns it.

tmdb_overview: Charlie goes into overdrive when he's notified that the health inspector will be arriving that day. Meanwhile, the rest of the gang is trying to exploit a flaw in the air-miles reward system.
